explanation.en: `Func<int, int, int>` and `Action<string>` are the built-in .NET delegate types, and `Console.WriteLine` with a `$"..."` interpolated string is classic C#.
`struct Point` is a C# value type: `var b = a` copies it, so changing `b.X` leaves `a.X` at 1. The object initializer `new Point { X = 1, Y = 2 }` and `Console.WriteLine` confirm C#.
The `[Flags]` attribute on an enum plus `HasFlag` is .NET; printing the combined value shows "Read, Write" because the flags formatter names each set bit.
`using static System.Math;` imports the static members of a class so `Sqrt` and `Pow` (and `WriteLine` from `System.Console`) can be called unqualified. Java spells this `import static`.
Format specifiers after a colon inside `$"{...}"` (`P1` percent, `D5` zero-padded, `X` hex) are .NET composite formatting in a C# interpolated string.
`Aggregate` is LINQ's fold (other languages call it reduce); with a seed of 0 it builds 407. LINQ and `Console.WriteLine` make it C#.
`GetType()` on an instance and the `typeof(...)` operator on a type are C# reflection entry points; they print "Int32" and "True".
`Path.Combine`, `File.ReadAllLines` and `AppContext.BaseDirectory` are .NET base class library APIs from System.IO, called from C#.
`Guid.NewGuid()`, `DateTime.UtcNow` and subtracting two DateTimes into a `TimeSpan` are .NET types used from C#; `{id:N}` formats the GUID without dashes.
`System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch` with `StartNew()` and `ElapsedMilliseconds` is the standard .NET way to time code in C#.
`using System.Text;` and `StringBuilder` with a writable `Length` property (here trimming the last comma with `sb.Length--`) are C#; Java would need `setLength`.
`HashSet<string>` with `StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase` is .NET; `Add` returns false for an existing item, so "the" and "CAT" are reported as duplicates.
`SelectMany` flattens nested sequences in LINQ; implicitly typed arrays `new[] { ... }` and `string.Join` are C#.
`@"..."` is a C# verbatim string: backslashes are literal, it may span lines, and a quote is written by doubling it (`""Ada""`).
The `event EventHandler?` field, subscribing with `+=` and raising with `?.Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty)` is the standard C# event pattern.
The `where T : new()` constraint lets generic code call `new T()`; C# reifies generics, which Java's type erasure does not allow.
`delegate decimal PriceRule(decimal price);` declares a named delegate type, and the `m` suffix makes a `decimal` literal: both are C#-only.
A static method whose first parameter is `this IEnumerable<T>` is a C# extension method, so it can be called as if it were a member of the array.
LINQ `GroupBy` followed by `ToDictionary(g => g.Key, ...)` turns groups into a `Dictionary<char, int>`; PascalCase LINQ methods and the collection initializer are C#.
`public double this[int row, int col]` declares an indexer, and `double[,]` is a rectangular multidimensional array: both are C# features.
`public static Money operator +(...)` overloads `+` on a `readonly struct` with a primary constructor; target-typed `new(...)` and `{Amount:C}` currency formatting are C#.
`abstract`, `virtual` and an explicit `override` keyword, inheritance written as `class Dog : Animal`, and `GetType().Name` mark this as C#.
`#nullable enable` turns on nullable reference types, so `string?` marks a parameter that may be null; `is { Length: > 0 }` is a property pattern and `name[..1]` a range.
A `switch` statement with type patterns (`case int i`), a `when` guard and `case null` is C# pattern matching.
The parameter modifiers `ref` (read-write by reference), `in` (read-only by reference) and `out` (must be assigned) are C#-specific.
An `async IAsyncEnumerable<int>` iterator that mixes `await` and `yield return`, consumed with `await foreach`, is a C# async stream.
The `lock` statement (on the .NET 9 `System.Threading.Lock` type) and `Parallel.For` with a `_` discard are C#; Java uses `synchronized` instead.
`Task.WhenAll` awaits a batch of tasks and returns their results as an `int[]`; async lambdas inside LINQ `Select` and top-level `await` are C#.
A `using var` declaration calls `Dispose()` automatically when the enclosing block ends; implementing `IDisposable` is the .NET resource-cleanup contract.
The `dynamic` type defers member binding to run time, and `ExpandoObject` lets you add properties on the fly: C# with the .NET dynamic language runtime.
`System.Text.Json.JsonSerializer.Serialize` with `JsonSerializerOptions` is .NET's built-in JSON library; the anonymous type `new { Name = ... }` is C#.
`Regex.Match` from System.Text.RegularExpressions with a verbatim `@"..."` pattern and a named group read via `m.Groups["id"]` is .NET regex in C#.
xUnit.net tests: `[Fact]` marks a test, `[Theory]` with `[InlineData]` a parameterised one, and `Assert.Equal(expected, actual)` checks the result. Square-bracket attributes are C#.
It looks like Java, but `public event Action<int>` declares a C# event backed by a delegate, and `onReading?.Invoke(value)` raises it only when someone has subscribed.
An `extension(string s) { ... }` block is C# 14's extension members syntax: it adds an extension property (`"text".WordCount`), which classic `this` extension methods could not.
The contextual keyword `field` (C# 14) refers to the compiler-generated backing field, so a property can keep an auto `get;` while adding logic to its setter.
`^1` is a C# index counted from the end (the last element) and `1..^1` a range that slices off the first and last items. Java would also write `String`, not `string`.
A Java-like interface, but the method body `=> area() * k * k` needs no `default` keyword: C# 8 default interface methods use an expression body, and `class Square : Shape` implements it.
Java-style naming, but `virtual`, `sealed override` (stop further overriding) and `base.execute()` are C#; Java would write `extends`, `@Override`, `final` and `super`.
`ref int` locals and `return ref` hand back a reference into the array, so a caller can assign through it (`Largest(xs) = 0`). Ref returns are a C# 7 feature.
Pointer code that looks like C, but `unsafe { }` and `fixed (int* p = data)` (pinning a managed array so the GC cannot move it) exist only in C#.
Java-style try/catch, but the `when (...)` exception filter and `unchecked((int)0x80070020)` are C#: the catch only runs when the HResult matches (a sharing violation).
Java has Queue and Stack too, but `Queue<int>` with a primitive type argument, the `[1, 2, 3]` collection expression, `Dequeue()` and the `Count` property are .NET/C#.
`stackalloc` allocates the buffer on the stack and `Span<int>`/`ReadOnlySpan<int>` view it without copying; slicing with `[2..]` is a C# range.
`(x, y) = (y, x)` swaps through a C# value tuple, and `pair.Item1` is the default name of a ValueTuple element; JavaScript would need `[x, y] = [y, x]`.
